transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-21 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sophie Li (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Velox Head ML), Tom Garrett (Velox SRE), Maya Ortiz (Velox CTO), Ben Cho (Velox Data Eng)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on a multi-tier reranking architecture: edge caching + vector DB fanout + model rerank step. Goals: pick hosting mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), quantify throughput & tail latency tradeoffs, and validate vector DB integration approach.

Topics covered:
- Target QPS/burst and latency SLOs
- Embedding dimensionality tradeoffs (128/256/512/1024) and quantization impact
- Vector DB choices and hybrid sparse+dense retrieval
- Multi-tier architecture (edge cache, regional dedicated pools, private failover)
- Security / compliance (KMS, SAML, audit logs)
- Next steps and perf tests

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, great to see you. Quick roll call—this is Lena from Redwood, Marco and Sophie joining on the infra side.
[00:08] Aisha Khan: Hi, Aisha here, thanks for doing this. We're trying to lock down where to run the rerank flow; we've got a big POC requirement and some regulatory constraints.
[00:15] Marco Ruiz: Nice to meet you all. To frame it: multi-tier means small edge cache for hot items, vector DB for recall, then a lightweight LLM rerank per top-k. We'll talk numbers.
[00:28] Tom Garrett: Our thing—SRE—main constraint is tail latency at the 99th. We run customer search that needs sub-150ms end-to-end for the majority of requests; burst to 2k QPS during promos. Typical steady is 250 QPS.
[00:42] Sophie Li: That helps. Are you planning dense-only embeddings or hybrid with BM25/sparse?
[00:47] Maya Ortiz: We're using BM25 for baseline, but the plan is hybrid. We want sparse candidate generation plus dense fanout to rerank. It reduces overall vector DB QPS.
[00:59] Ben Cho: Also want to experiment with 128 vs 512 dimensions to see cost/precision tradeoffs.
[01:06] Lena Park: Perfect. Quick question on dataset size—how many documents?
[01:10] Aisha Khan: ~190M product descriptions, but only ~20M active items; the rest are historical.
[01:16] Marco Ruiz: Ok, so sharding and HNSW index sizing matters. For 20M active points, 512-d will be a different cost envelope than 128-d. Rough back-of-envelope: 512-d unquantized vectors at 20M means a lot of memory across shards.
[01:30] Tom Garrett: From infra, we prefer not to expose internal data—so Private deployment or Dedicated w/ VPC peering are on the table. Hosted is ok for non-PII workloads.
[01:40] Lena Park: Right, security callouts matter: Redwood Private supports on-prem or VPC modal, KMS/HSM integrations, SAML SSO and audit logs. We'll send SOC2 artifacts.
[01:50] Maya Ortiz: Important—SAML and audit logs for compliance. Also interested in token-level cost breakdowns for the rerank LLM.
[01:58] Sophie Li: We'll include cost per rerank call in the workbook. For architecture, low-latency path is edge cache for top N queries, then vector DB fanout with async fallback to a slightly cheaper model.
[02:13] Aisha Khan: Can you explain fanout and rerank latency math? We want expected p95 under 120ms for satisfied results.
[02:20] Marco Ruiz: Sure—example flow: client -> edge cache (fast, <10ms) for 30% hit. Miss -> query vector DB (HNSW) ~20-40ms depending on neighbors & shard colocation -> retrieve top 100 dense candidates -> lightweight rerank LLM call on top 10. The rerank is the costly bit for cost + latency.
[02:41] Tom Garrett: Is rerank done synchronously? If we do synchronous LLM on top10, that's X ms per call times concurrency. Could we do async and optimistic UI?
[02:50] Sophie Li: You can do async UX but many product teams prefer synchronous so result is deterministic. Redwood supports both patterns; for sync we recommend an optimized smaller model (1-2 token calls?) or batching rerank calls.
[03:05] Ben Cho: Batching rerank—how does Redwood do batching across requests while keeping latency SLO?
[03:11] Marco Ruiz: The runtime does continuous batching but will respect latency SLOs per route. You configure target latency, and it will trade off batch size. For dedicated pools you get more predictable batching behavior.
[03:23] Aisha Khan: What about quantization? We were looking at int8 or 4-bit for embeddings to save memory. Does that impact similarity quality?
[03:31] Marco Ruiz: Quantization helps with memory and throughput on GPU-backed vector indexes. For embeddings 128 vs 512, quantization tends to hurt less on lower dims for certain ANN backends, but it depends on your precision needs. We'll try A/B: 128d int8 vs 512d fp16.
[03:48] Maya Ortiz: And end-to-end cost? We need numbers to compare Hosted token cost + vector DB external costs vs Dedicated reserved capacity.
[03:56] Lena Park: We'll provide a spreadsheet that models per-request cost: edge hit rate, vector DB cost (if you use a managed vector DB like Pinecone or self-host), rerank model cost, and dedicated slot amortization.
[04:07] Tom Garrett: On vector DB—do you recommend managed services or self-hosted Milvus/Weaviate? We already run Elasticsearch clusters; adding another managed product is operational overhead.
[04:16] Sophie Li: Common patterns: 1) Managed vector DB (Pinecone/others) for quick go-to-market; 2) Self-hosted Milvus or Vespa for tight control; 3) Use Redwood Dedicated to co-locate vector indexes on the same VPC for lower network hop. Each has tradeoffs for maintenance, SLA, and cost.
[04:33] Ben Cho: If we keep index local to Redwood Dedicated, does Redwood handle sharding and autoscale?
[04:38] Marco Ruiz: Yes, Redwood Dedicated supports autoscaling policies and shard placement are part of the infra plan. We can size initial pool to match 250 steady QPS with headroom for bursts and then recommend burst capacity.
[04:50] Aisha Khan: Tail latency target we're aiming for p99 <150ms end-to-end. Can Redwood meet that with synchronous rerank?
[04:57] Marco Ruiz: With Dedicated and model choices (quantized smaller reranker) plus edge cache and regional placement we can get p95 in 80-120ms and p99 in 150-250ms depending on model. If you need hard p99 <150ms, we recommend moving rerank to a smaller distilled model or doing partial async UX.
[05:18] Maya Ortiz: Ok, what about fallback when vector DB is overloaded?
[05:21] Sophie Li: Redwood has smart routing and automatic fallback to compatible model variants or to a cheaper retrieval-only path. For example, if dense fanout degrades, fallback to sparse-only or to a cached rerank.
[05:33] Tom Garrett: Network and security—VPC peering acceptable? We need to control ingress/egress and key management.
[05:39] Lena Park: Yes. For Dedicated we support VPC peering and Private supports customer-managed networking and HSM/KMS integration. We'll share a network diagram and the private deployment checklist.
[05:50] Aisha Khan: Any benchmarks you can share for 512d vs 128d with HNSW?
[05:55] Marco Ruiz: We have internal benchmarks; they'll be in the workbook. Rough rule: 512d gives better recall but 2-4x memory and slower ANN ops. 128d is much cheaper and faster but sometimes needs better rerank to recover precision. We'll run a small dimension sweep for your data.
[06:11] Ben Cho: How will you run the sweep? We want to replicate our latencies not synthetic.
[06:14] Marco Ruiz: We'll ask for a representative subset you send. We'll run tests on Hosted and on a Dedicated-sized pool to compare p95/p99 and cost. We'll log network hops and KV cache hit rates.
[06:25] Aisha Khan: Can Redwood's KV/prefix cache be used to store recent reranks? That might cut rerank calls.
[06:30] Sophie Li: Yes, we support prefix/KV caching. Hot queries can be served from cache which dramatically reduces LLM rerank costs.
[06:37] Lena Park: To be explicit on deliverables—Marco will run perf test on 128/512 dims on Hosted and share p95/p99 + cost per 1k requests. We'll also give a Dedicated sizing workbook.
[06:47] Maya Ortiz: Good. Also please include security docs and SOC2 evidence.
[06:51] Lena Park: Will do. We'll also include a diagram for multi-tier routing: edge cache -> vector DB (fanout) -> rerank -> fallback.
[06:59] Tom Garrett: If we decide Private, how long to deploy?
[07:02] Marco Ruiz: Private (VPC kit) is typically 4-8 weeks depending on networking approvals; Dedicated is faster—2-3 weeks for initial pool provisioning. Hosted is immediate.
[07:12] Aisha Khan: Budget-level question—what's typical for dedicated commit for this scale?
[07:16] Lena Park: Depends on sizing. For a 250 QPS steady with bursts and 20M active points, we usually see reserved capacity commitments in the mid-six figures annually, but the spreadsheet will break that down.
[07:27] Ben Cho: Any gotchas around embedding dimension interoperability with our existing vector pipeline? We use a preprocessor that normalizes to 0 mean currently.
[07:34] Sophie Li: Normalization is fine; ensure you standardize on the embedding model. Changing models changes index semantics and recall. Redwood's eval and rollout features help pin model versions and guardrails.
[07:46] Aisha Khan: Can you do an A/B on hosting modes to show delta?
[07:50] Marco Ruiz: Yes—pilot plan: run the same workload on Hosted and on a Dedicated pilot pool and compare latency/cost. We'll instrument with tracing for per-route token cost and vector DB ops.
[08:01] Lena Park: Alright let's confirm next steps.
[08:03] Lena Park: Action recap - Lena send workbook and SOC2; Marco run perf tests 128/512 dims; Aisha provide sample data; Tom share VPC diagram. Schedule infra deep-dive.
[08:15] Aisha Khan: That works. One more small question—are you able to integrate with our existing Elasticsearch as hybrid candidate source?
[08:21] Sophie Li: Yes, Redwood can accept multiple candidate sources. We often do hybrid retrieval: BM25 from ES + dense recall from vector DB and then rerank.
[08:30] Maya Ortiz: Great. Thanks everyone, we look forward to the workbook.
[08:33] Lena Park: Thanks, we'll follow up with the links. Deck and workbook references: deck: https://app.redwood.ai/decks/multi-tier-rerank (shared), workbook: https://sheets.redwood.ai/velox-poc-sizing (benchmark spreadsheet).
[08:45] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcript quirks: occasional mis-typed acronyms (VP C instead of VPC), 'K V cache' spelled out, and small disfluencies left in to preserve authenticity.
